opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think about it a lot. Longer context windows have been one of the more surprising wins of the last couple of years. Going from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands, even millions, changes what you can do. You can drop a whole codebase or a long video or a stack of documents into the model, and it can attend over all of it. That's very powerful, and in a way it removed some of the pressure to build clever memory systems, because the brute-force approach just worked better than many people expected.

But I don't think long context makes hierarchical memory obsolete. If anything, it changes what memory is for. A context window, however long, is still a flat buffer. Everything sits at the same level, and the model has to work out on the fly what matters. That's expensive, both computationally and in terms of the model's ability to reason precisely over everything at once. Humans don't work like that. We have working memory, which is tiny, then episodic memories, then semantic, more abstracted knowledge. And we're constantly compressing. You don't remember every word of a conversation from last week, but you remember the gist, the decisions, maybe a key phrase.

So I see the value of hierarchy in a few places. First, efficiency. Even if you can fit ten million tokens, you may not want to pay to attend over all of them on every step. Summaries and abstractions at different time scales let you be selective. Second, persistence. As we move toward agents that operate over days, weeks, or months, interacting with you, writing code, running experiments, no context window is going to hold all of that. You need some way to consolidate experience into something more durable. Third, and I think this is the most interesting from a research perspective, abstraction itself is a form of understanding. When you compress an experience into a higher-level memory, you're deciding what was important, and that act of distillation is close to learning.

There's a broader question underneath this, which is where the line between memory and weights should be. Right now we have pre-training, which puts knowledge into the weights, and then context, which is very transient. There's a big gap in between. Hierarchical memory, whether it's explicit retrieval structures, learned compression, or some form of continual learning that updates the model gradually, is one way to fill that gap.

So my view is that long context and hierarchical memory are complementary. Long context gives you a very capable working memory, and hierarchical structures give you the long-term part. I'd expect the most capable systems to use both, and the design space for how they interact is still pretty open.

r001.rationale: The response says that summaries and abstractions at different time scales enable selective attention for efficiency, but it does not clearly identify coarse-to-fine memory retrieval as the source of that efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response directly.

Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one where my intuition has actually shifted a bit over the last couple of years. Early on, when context windows were, you know, two thousand tokens, four thousand tokens, the whole game was compression. You had to decide what mattered and throw the rest away, and so hierarchies felt almost mandatory. You'd have some fast, short-term buffer, and then some slower, more abstract summary, and then maybe a retrieval layer on top of that. And that's quite biologically inspired too, right? Working memory, episodic memory, semantic memory, and so on.

Now we're at a point where a model can just read a million tokens, or more, and attend over all of it. And the naive reaction is, okay, hierarchy is dead, just put everything in the window. But I don't think that's right, for a couple of reasons.

The first is that the context window is not the same as memory. The window is more like what's on your desk right now. It's extremely useful, it's very precise, you can look at every detail. But it's expensive to keep everything on the desk, and more importantly, it resets. The moment the conversation ends, or the agent moves to a new task, that's gone unless you've written it somewhere. So you still need some notion of what persists across episodes, and that is inherently a different layer.

The second is that even within a very long context, attention is not free in a practical sense. There's compute cost, obviously, but there's also a sort of signal-to-noise problem. If I give you ten million tokens of someone's email history and ask a question, the relevant piece is maybe a few hundred tokens. The model has to find it. And the longer the context, the harder it is to not get distracted by things that look superficially relevant. So having some structure, some index, some coarser representation that says "roughly, this region is about this topic," helps a lot. That's hierarchy again, just maybe learned rather than hand-designed.

And then there's the point about abstraction, which I think is the most interesting one. If you've been working with an agent for a year, you don't want it to re-read a year of logs every time. You want it to have distilled things. "This user prefers concise answers." "This codebase has this convention." Those are compressed facts that came from a huge amount of raw experience, and you want them at the top of the hierarchy, cheap to access, while the raw experience sits lower down, available if you really need to go back and check.

So the way I'd put it is, longer context windows change where the boundaries between the levels sit. The bottom level gets much bigger, and that's fantastic because a lot of the hacks we used to do, chunking documents, clever retrieval tricks, you can just skip them. But the levels above it don't go away. If anything, as agents become long-lived and operate over months, the question of what to keep, what to summarize, and what to forget becomes more important, not less. And honestly, I'd love for more of that to be learned end to end rather than engineered. The model should figure out what's worth remembering. We're not fully there yet, but I think that's where it's going.

r001.rationale: The response says a coarse representation can direct the model to relevant regions, then leaves raw details available when needed, making retrieval more efficient.

astra-6.text:
I think longer context windows and hierarchical memory are complementary. A longer context window lets you put more information in front of the model, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what’s worth remembering or what’s relevant right now.

Imagine an agent working with you for years. You probably don’t want it to reread every interaction each time you ask a question. You want it to retain useful summaries, retrieve particular details when they matter, and be able to go back to the original experience if a summary has lost something important.

The interesting question is how much of that structure we should design and how much the model can learn. Summarizing is lossy, so deciding what to keep is itself an intelligence problem. Longer contexts give us more room to postpone that decision, which is very useful. But I don’t think they eliminate the need to organize memory.

r001.rationale: It describes using summaries first, retrieving specific details when needed, and avoiding rereading every interaction, which communicates coarse-to-fine retrieval as an efficiency benefit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think longer context windows and hierarchical memory are complementary. Even if you could put everything into the context, you still have to decide what matters. If we’ve been talking for an hour, you probably don’t need to remember every word equally well. You want the main ideas, and then the ability to go back to the details when they become relevant.

So I wouldn’t think of hierarchy only as a workaround for a small context window. It’s also a way to organize information across different timescales. Some things are useful for the next few seconds; others should influence how you behave months later. The interesting question is how much of that organization the model can learn: what to keep, what to summarize, and when to retrieve the original information.

Longer context gives you more room to work with, which is great. But it doesn’t automatically solve those decisions.

r001.rationale: The response describes keeping main ideas and retrieving details when relevant, which conveys coarse-to-fine retrieval. It does not identify that approach as a source of efficiency.
